title: Tears of the Mothers
body:
PART VIII: THE PATH OF TRANSCENDENCE

Tears of the Mothers

The physical clatter of Kurukshetra lay frozen. The 18-day holocaust, which swept away eleven divisions of the Kauravas and seven of the Pandavas, had finally resolved itself into a silent, blood-soaked waste of bones and ashes. Into this agonizing wilderness of grief, King Dhritarashtra trudged wearily, his blind eyes weeping uselessly for the hundred sons he had sacrificed to his doting attachment and political greed. Beside him walked Queen Gandhari, her eyes forever sheathed in her blindfold, accompanied by many thousands of bereaved royal women whose loud lamentations rent the stagnant sky. The mighty Kurukshetra field, once a pageant of proud banners, now lay as a grotesque monument to human ego.
Sanjaya, the faithful minister whose divine vision had dissolved with the termination of the war, stood by the blind king. Seeking to bring solace to a mind consumed by remorse, Sanjaya addressed the weeping monarch: 'O King, words of consolation addressed to a bereaved person do not remove his grief. Thousands of rulers have given up their lives in battle for your sons. It is now time that you should arrange for the proper funeral ceremonies for the dead.'
The great sage Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, the progenitor and detached witness of the Kuru line, approached Dhritarashtra tenderly. With a voice reflecting the profound depths of the Upanishads, Vyasa sought to lift the king's consciousness from the physical shell of grief to the eternal plane of the soul: 'Dear son, there is nothing that you do not know and which you have to learn from me. You know very well that all living beings must die. This great battle came to reduce earth's burden, as I have heard from Lord Vishnu Himself. That is why this calamity could not be prevented. Henceforth, Yudhishthira is your son. You should try to love him and in that way bear the burden of life, giving up grief.'
Yudhishthira, now the undisputed monarch of a desolated empire, approached his blind uncle through the weeping crowds. As he bowed in deep reverence, seeking a father's embrace, the underlying tension of the war still lingered. Though Dhritarashtra opened his arms to clasp Yudhishthira, there was no love in that embrace. It was the heavy, physical embrace of an elder bound to the laws of family, but internally burning with the unresolved embers of grief for Duryodhana and Dushasana.
